items.reference_answer: By default, the calendar heatmap displays times in UTC. The displayed time for each cell and the starting day of the week are based on your project's date and time settings, so you can change the timezone in your project settings (under the date and time section).

items.question: If I remove an insight from one of my dashboards, does it get deleted from PostHog entirely? I want to clean up without accidentally losing it.
items.reference_answer: No. Removing an insight only removes it from the current dashboard. The insight still exists in PostHog and on any other dashboards where it appears. To delete it permanently, use the 'Delete insight everywhere' option in the toast notification, which removes it from PostHog and every dashboard it appears on. That option opens a confirmation dialog listing other dashboards that use the insight, and deletion can be undone after confirming. 'Delete insight everywhere' only appears if you have editor access; users with view access can remove the insight from the dashboard but won't see the delete option.

items.question: PostHog AI keeps giving me the wrong results when I ask about signups. What should I change in how I phrase my requests?
items.reference_answer: The guidance includes several changes: name your events explicitly (e.g., 'Show me `user_signed_up` events' works better than 'show me signups' if PostHog AI can't match the event name); specify time ranges such as 'in the last 30 days' or 'this week'; describe the visualization you want, such as 'as a funnel' or 'broken down by browser'; iterate with follow-ups to adjust filters, add breakdowns, or change the chart type after the initial insight is created; and ask questions rather than just giving commands, such as 'What changed this week?' or 'Why did signups drop?', which prompt PostHog AI to investigate and explain rather than only build a chart.

items.question: When I call evaluateFlags in the Node SDK, what does the onlyEvaluateLocally option do, and what is its default value?
items.reference_answer: The onlyEvaluateLocally option controls whether PostHog makes a server request when it can't evaluate a flag locally. It defaults to false. Setting it to true means PostHog will not make a server request if it can't evaluate the flag locally.

items.question: We need to rotate our feature flags secure API key without breaking production. How do we do that, and when can we delete the old key?
items.reference_answer: Key rotation generates new keys while keeping the old one temporarily active. During the transition, the primary and backup keys are both maintained, which allows a rotation without downtime. Once all your systems use the new key, you delete the backup key. These keys are managed in Settings > Feature flags.

items.question: My feature flag returned a value I didn't expect for one of my users. Is the flag misbehaving, or should I be looking somewhere else?
items.reference_answer: The flag itself is usually fine. Evaluating the same flag with the same distinct ID always returns the same result because the hash is deterministic. When a flag returns an unexpected value, the problem is almost always in the inputs passed to the flag, such as the identity, the properties, or the flag definition. You should find what changed in those inputs.

items.question: I'm using OpenFeature with the Node.js server SDK. How do I set up PostHog and evaluate a boolean flag, and do I need to clean anything up when my app stops?
items.reference_answer: Create a PostHog client from 'posthog-node' with your project API key and host. Register it by calling await OpenFeature.setProviderAndWait(new PostHogServerProvider(posthog)), where PostHogServerProvider comes from '@posthog/openfeature-node-provider'. Get a client with OpenFeature.getClient(), then evaluate the flag with await client.getBooleanValue('my-flag', false, { targetingKey: 'user_distinct_id' }). The targetingKey supplies the distinct ID, and resolution returns a promise. You own the PostHog client lifecycle, so call posthog.shutdown() when your app exits. The chunk also shows a commented-out personalApiKey option that enables local evaluation.

items.question: Before I launch an A/B test, what should I check about exposure events, and when should the exposure event fire?
items.reference_answer: Before launching, confirm that exposure events are being sent correctly for all variants. Place the exposure event at the moment users actually encounter the experimental change, not just when they load a page or app. Monitor exposure balance to check that users are distributed across variants according to your configured percentages, since significant imbalances may indicate implementation issues. If you use custom exposure events, document what triggers them and any required properties.

items.question: Which statistical test does PostHog use for frequentist experiment results, and how is the p-value calculated?
items.reference_answer: PostHog uses Welch's t-test, a two-sided test that handles unequal variances between groups. The null hypothesis (H₀) is that there is no difference (effect_size = 0). The p-value is calculated as 2 × (1 − t_cdf(|t_statistic|, degrees_of_freedom)), using the cumulative distribution function of the t-distribution, with degrees of freedom from the Welch-Satterthwaite approximation.

items.question: I only want to record a percentage of the sessions in a trigger group, and I want to ignore very short sessions. How can I do that?
items.reference_answer: Use two controls on the trigger group. For the percentage, set the group's sampling sample rate (for example, 0.1 for 10% or 0.2 for 20%). PostHog applies it to the sessions that match that group's conditions. Selection is deterministic, based on a hash of the session ID, so you can't choose which specific sessions are sampled. To ignore very short sessions, set a minimum duration in your replay ingestion settings (for example, 2 seconds). Each trigger group has its own minimum duration. Sampling requires posthog-js 1.85.0+ on web, and minimum duration requires posthog-js 1.291.0+ on web. Mobile SDKs have their own minimum versions.
items.notes: Source: session-replay/how-to-control-which-sessions-you-record.mdx#2 | Title: Controls available | Headings: How to control which sessions you record > Trigger groups > Controls available

items.question: Which Cisco Meraki tables sync incrementally, and which ones do a full refresh on every sync?
items.reference_answer: Only `network_events` is incremental, syncing only new data since the last sync. The other six tables (`networks`, `devices`, `inventory_devices`, `uplink_statuses`, `assurance_alerts`, and `network_clients`) use full refresh, which reloads all data on each sync.

items.question: I'm connecting Mintlify as a data source in PostHog. Which of its tables sync incrementally, and what field do they use to track new or updated records?
items.reference_answer: Only the assistant_conversations table syncs incrementally. It uses the timestamp field as a cursor, so each run syncs only new or updated records. The feedback, searches, views, and visitors tables use full refresh, which reloads all data on each sync. Feedback uses full refresh because its status can change without a modification timestamp. Searches, views, and visitors use full refresh because they contain aggregates rather than individual events.

items.question: I'm building a SQL insight that groups events by time period. How can I make the time grouping follow the dashboard's interval setting, and what happens if I don't pass an argument to the placeholder?
items.reference_answer: Use the placeholder {filters.interval('week')} wherever the time unit goes, such as the first argument to dateTrunc. At runtime it is replaced with the dashboard's interval as a string constant, such as 'week'. The argument you pass sets the default used when the dashboard doesn't set an interval. If you omit the argument, the default is 'day'. Valid intervals are second, minute, hour, day, week, month, quarter, and year.

items.question: My data quality check on the events table keeps timing out. What should I do first, and does an errored check count as a failing assertion?
items.reference_answer: First, open the run's error details before you change the assertion. Common causes include invalid HogQL, a renamed column, a missing table, changed permissions, an unsupported metric definition, or a query timeout. For large events, persons, or groups checks, turn on "Only check recent rows"; events filters on timestamp, while persons and groups filter on created_at. Use the smallest window that still tests the data your decision depends on. An errored check does not count as a failing assertion. If the materialization gate is on, query errors and audit failures don't guarantee a block.
items.notes: Source: data-warehouse/data-quality/troubleshooting.mdx#6 | Title: Fix query errors and timeouts | Headings: Data quality results and troubleshooting > Fix query errors and timeouts

items.question: When I call analytics.group() in Segment, the company shows up under a segment_group type in PostHog. How can I associate events with a company group type instead, and do I need to set it on every event?

items.question: What should I send with a 'Coupon Entered' event, and when should it fire?
items.reference_answer: Fire the Coupon Entered event when a coupon is entered on a cart or order. It has three properties: order_id (String, the order or transaction ID, if applicable), cart_id (String, the cart ID, if applicable), and coupon_id (String, the coupon ID). For example, posthog.capture('Coupon Entered', { order_id: 'a239ebb8404c4ac29950756f', cart_id: 'cb271d41bc2140ea8d076c50', coupon_id: 'blackfriday_2025' }).

items.question: I'm seeing ingestion warnings in my PostHog project. Does that mean the affected events were thrown away, and can I use the count shown to tell how often this is happening?
items.reference_answer: Not necessarily. Where possible, PostHog still ingests the event and logs an ingestion warning. Other problems leave nothing to ingest, and the warning is then the only record. The warnings are sampled, so the number of affected events may exceed the total displayed. The count should be used to confirm that something is happening, not to measure how often it happens. An example of an event that is not ingested is one captured with a generic ID such as null.
items.notes: Source: data/ingestion-warnings.mdx#0 | Title: Ingestion warnings | Headings: Ingestion warnings

items.question: What exactly are UTM parameters, and what does a tagged URL look like?
items.reference_answer: UTM parameters are a set of five parameters that let you track the effectiveness of marketing campaigns across traffic sources. They were first introduced by Google Analytics and are now a common way to identify where website traffic comes from. They are appended to a URL as query parameters, for example: https://www.example.com/page?utm_source=twitter&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=twitter-campaign. Nearly every ad platform sets them when sending traffic to your website, and you can also set them yourself.
items.notes: Source: data/utm-segmentation.mdx#0 | Title: UTM segmentation | Headings: UTM segmentation

items.question: I'm building embedded analytics and want a separate project for each customer. How do I create those projects, how do I query a customer's data afterward, and how many projects can a free organization have?
items.reference_answer: You create a project when you add a customer by calling the projects API. Each project has its own project token for event ingestion. To query a customer's data, you use that project's ID when calling Endpoints or the Query API. Free organizations are limited to one project, while the Boost plan includes unlimited projects. Note that analyzing data across all customers is harder with this setup, because PostHog queries are scoped to one project, so you would need to query each project separately and combine the results.

items.question: Our team is shipping a risky new checkout flow. We want to first expose it to a small subset of users, watch error rates and usage metrics, and widen the rollout only once we're satisfied. We also want beta testers to opt themselves in and out. Can we use early access feature management for both goals if our rollout targets company-level Groups and the feature is gated in our Python backend?
items.reference_answer: Not for this combination. Early access feature management is only available in the JavaScript Web SDK and does not support Groups, so it can't handle group-level targeting or gate a feature in a Python backend. The staged-exposure goal is a canary release: a new feature goes to a subset of users before a larger group, developers watch for issues and analyze usage metrics, and then the feature rolls out to a larger group or everyone. That process has to be run through a different rollout approach for company-level targeting. The beta opt-in goal matches early access management's purpose, which lets users opt in and out at different development stages through beta programs and waitlists. That works only for individual users in the JavaScript Web SDK, so it covers the user-controlled beta piece for web front-end users at most.
items.notes:
Synthesized from:
  - Chunk 1: feature-flags/early-access-feature-management.mdx#0 (https://posthog.com/docs/feature-flags/early-access-feature-management)
  - Chunk 2: feature-flags/canary-release.md#1 (https://posthog.com/docs/feature-flags/canary-release)
Rationale: Chunk 1 supplies the constraints (JavaScript Web SDK only, no Groups support) and the purpose of early access management (user opt-in across development stages, beta programs, waitlists). Chunk 2 defines canary release as a staged subset-then-wider rollout with monitoring of issues and usage metrics. Answering requires checking the canary rollout pattern against the early access constraints. Chunk 1 alone does not explain what a canary release is or why staged exposure matters, and Chunk 2 alone says nothing about SDK or Group restrictions. Only the combination shows that early access can cover opt-in betas for web users but cannot serve as the group-targeted, Python-backed canary mechanism.

items.question: Our team is about to launch a checkout experiment. Before we go live, I want to confirm that my colleagues and I actually see the test variant when we visit the site, including when we're logged out. I also need to know how long the experiment has to run to get reliable results. What steps should I take for each of these, and what inputs determine the running time?
items.reference_answer: To verify variants before launch, add an optional override to your experiment's feature flag rather than relying only on the code. Open the flag, make sure the 'Enable feature flag' box is checked, and add a new condition set with the condition email = your_email@domain.com (your own or a teammate's address) at a 100% rollout. Because email isn't available for logged-out users, use a parameter such as utm_source and append ?utm_source=your_variant_name to the URL. Then set the optional override to the variant you want those users to see, click Save, and confirm each variant behaves as expected. Only launch once this checks out, since a bug found after launch means the results can no longer be trusted and days of effort are lost. For running time, use the running time calculator before running the experiment. It estimates how long the experiment needs to run based on your traffic and the size of the effect you want to detect. Lower traffic or a smaller effect to detect generally means a longer run.
items.notes:
Synthesized from:
  - Chunk 1: experiments/testing-and-launching.mdx#0 (https://posthog.com/docs/experiments/testing-and-launching)
  - Chunk 2: experiments/sample-size-running-time.mdx#0 (https://posthog.com/docs/experiments/sample-size-running-time)
Rationale: Chunk 1 supplies the pre-launch verification procedure: the email-based override condition at 100% rollout, the utm_source fallback for logged-out users, the optional variant override, saving, and the rule to launch only after testing. It does not explain how long the experiment should run. Chunk 2 supplies the running-time calculator and its inputs (traffic and target effect size) but says nothing about testing or overrides. The question combines both pre-launch steps, so a complete answer needs the QA workflow from Chunk 1 and the duration estimation from Chunk 2. The statement that smaller effects and lower traffic lengthen runs is general statistical reasoning, not stated explicitly in either chunk. Chunk 2's image references carry no usable text, so the answer relies only on its prose.

items.question: Our app renders a WebGL-based data visualization that we want to see in session replays so we can debug user issues. Before we turn that on, what do we need to verify about our PostHog JS SDK version and our PII exposure, and how should we think about keeping our Session Replay bill under control?
items.reference_answer:
For canvas capture, you need PostHog JS SDK v1.105.7 or later. Canvas support was added in that version, and canvas capture won't work on older versions. PostHog can capture WebGL canvases (as well as 2D), but canvas content is not covered by DOM-based masking, so PostHog doesn't capture canvas elements automatically. Before enabling it, confirm the canvas is free of PII, or set up canvas masking. Then enable canvas recording globally in your project's replay settings. Canvas elements are recorded at 4 frames per second, so playback may look less smooth than normal replay.

For cost, Session Replay is free up to a monthly allowance of web and mobile recordings, then billed per recording with volume discounts. There are no per-seat charges. You can set a billing limit so a traffic spike can't cause a surprise bill. Recording rules and data retention are the two biggest levers on your bill, so you can tune them to control spend. The docs don't say that canvas recording changes pricing, so the cost controls come from the general billing model.
items.notes:
Synthesized from:
  - Chunk 1: session-replay/start-here.mdx#2 (https://posthog.com/docs/session-replay/start-here)
  - Chunk 2: session-replay/canvas-recording.mdx#0 (https://posthog.com/docs/session-replay/canvas-recording)
Rationale: Chunk 2 alone covers the canvas requirements: the SDK version floor (v1.105.7), the fact that canvas isn't covered by DOM masking so it must be verified PII-free or masked before enabling, where to enable it (replay settings), and the 4 fps recording rate. It says nothing about pricing or billing controls. Chunk 1 alone covers the billing model: the free monthly allowance, per-recording pricing with volume discounts, no per-seat charges, the billing limit, and recording rules and data retention as the main cost levers. It says nothing about canvas. A complete answer to the question requires both: the developer has to combine the canvas enablement prerequisites from Chunk 2 with the cost-management guidance from Chunk 1. The answer also notes that the docs don't link canvas recording to pricing, which avoids inventing a cost relationship the sources don't state.

items.question: Our team ships an Android app and wants a User Paths report showing how users move between screens. Will navigation data be captured by default without custom instrumentation, and how should we read the bars and numbers in the resulting paths chart?
items.reference_answer: On Android, PostHog's autocapture enables navigation, lifecycle, and deep-link autocapture by default, so screen-to-screen navigation is captured without custom instrumentation. Interaction autocapture (tap-level events) is not supported on Android, so the path steps will reflect screens rather than individual button taps. In the User Paths chart, each step is a page or screen the user viewed. The horizontal bars show a user navigating from one step to the next. The number next to each step is the count of distinct users who passed through that step, not the count of events.

items.question: Our onboarding survey has partial responses enabled. We want a Slack message for each response, including people who drop off partway through. What steps set up the Slack alerts, what default must we change to include partial submissions, and what happens to the open-text comments on the Self-driving side?

Choose Slack, select the channel, and customize the message template using the quick insert buttons for the survey name, respondent details, or individual question responses. Click Add notification. These notifications are automatically scoped to the current survey and by default only fire for completed submissions. Because the survey has partial responses enabled, you can turn off the 'Only notify for full responses' toggle so partial submissions also trigger alerts. For Slack, you can also add buttons that link to the survey and the respondent's person profile. For deeper customization, open the notification from the notifications list and use the full Hog function editor. On the Self-driving side, a dedicated scout clusters open-text answers into recurring themes and also watches active surveys for score regressions and abandonment spikes. Each validated theme becomes one report in the inbox, and that report goes to a human reviewer, not a coding agent. PostHog does not automatically turn comments into engineering fixes, because deciding how to respond to user sentiment is a product decision. The Slack alerts are per-response notifications, and the documentation does not say they feed into the theme clustering.

items.question: Our product has a React web frontend built with Vite and a separate Android app that includes NDK native code. We want readable stack traces in PostHog for both. What do we need to configure for each platform, and what should our Android release process account for so that crashes stay symbolicated?
items.reference_answer:
Web (React + Vite): In vite.config.js, keep the react() plugin and set `build: { sourcemap: true }`. For other bundlers such as webpack or Rollup, follow that tool's own source map docs. Then confirm in dev tools that the production files served to browsers include the `//# chunkId=...` source map comment.

Android: In build.gradle.kts, add `posthog { uploadNativeSymbols.set(true) }`. The Gradle plugin's uploadPostHogNativeSymbols task then uploads every unstripped native library that has debug info and a build ID, automatically after assemble, install, or bundle. This covers NDK-built code and .so files from jniLibs or dependencies, for both minified and non-minified builds. Debuggable variants are skipped by default. To get source context around crash frames, also set `includeNativeSymbolSources.set(true)`. You can run ./gradlew uploadPostHogNativeSymbolsRelease explicitly for any variant, or upload a directory of .so files with posthog-cli symbol-sets upload --directory <path>.

Release process: PostHog matches native frames to symbols by the GNU build ID that the NDK emits by default. Every build has its own build ID, so symbols must be re-uploaded for each build you ship. Native crash events are captured on the next app launch, so $app_version may show the version at capture time rather than the version that crashed. If the app updated in between, identify the crashing release by build ID instead of relying on the event's version properties.
items.notes:
Synthesized from:
  - Chunk 1: error-tracking/upload-source-maps/react.mdx#0 (https://posthog.com/docs/error-tracking/upload-source-maps/react)
  - Chunk 2: error-tracking/upload-mappings/android.mdx#1 (https://posthog.com/docs/error-tracking/upload-mappings/android)
Rationale: Chunk 1 covers only the web side: enabling source maps in a Vite config and verifying the chunkId source map comment. It says nothing about Android, Gradle, NDK, or build IDs. Chunk 2 covers only the Android side: the posthog Gradle configuration, the upload task behavior, build-ID matching, and the version-attribution caveat. It says nothing about React, Vite, or web source maps. A complete answer to the two-platform question needs the Vite configuration and verification step from Chunk 1 together with the Android upload setup and release-process guidance from Chunk 2. The answer also has to combine the two platforms' different mechanisms (source map comments for web, build-ID-matched native symbols for Android) into one coherent setup and release plan. Neither chunk alone yields the full answer.

items.question: We've synced our Stripe charges into PostHog and want revenue per user next to their product activity in one SQL query. The synced amount column comes through as a string, so my arithmetic on it doesn't work. How do I get this working, and where can I check the column types before writing the query?
items.reference_answer: PostHog's data warehouse lets you sync sources like Stripe and query them alongside events, persons, and sessions in a single SQL query, with no separate ETL pipeline or second analytics tool. To confirm the column types and names, check the Database and Properties tabs in Data management, or the SQL tab for external sources. STRING is the default type, so a synced amount column showing as STRING is expected. Convert it before doing math, for example with toFloat(amount) (or toInt / JSONExtractInt for integer and JSON-nested values), then aggregate, such as sum(toFloat(amount)) grouped by user, and join to events on the user identifier. Once the query works, you can save it as a view or materialized view and chart it in insights.

In PostHog, go to the sources tab in the data pipeline section, click + New source, and click Link next to Slash. Then select the tables to sync, choose the sync method and frequency, and click Import. For Postmark, select the bounces schema, which contains email bounces and delivery failures. items.question: Our marketing site is built in Webflow and our backend is written in PHP. When a visitor submits a form on the site, we want the backend to record an identified event in PostHog for that person, set their name as a person property, and record their landing page as initial_url only the first time we see them. Where should we look for the Webflow-side setup, and what PHP calls should the backend use?
items.reference_answer: For the Webflow side, start with the tutorial 'How to capture Webflow form submissions' (/tutorials/webflow-form-submissions). For other technical questions about integrating PostHog features into Webflow, such as analytics, feature flags, A/B testing, or surveys, use the JavaScript Web SDK docs (/docs/libraries/js/usage). For the backend, use the PHP SDK. The PHP SDK captures identified events by default, and these create person profiles. To record the submission for the visitor, call PostHog::capture with the visitor's distinctId, an event name, and a properties array containing '$set' => ['name' => ...] to set the name person property, and '$set_once' => ['initial_url' => ...] so initial_url is written only if it isn't already set. Alternatively, PostHog::identify with the distinctId and a properties array (for example email and name) sets person properties without a separate event. Do not set '$process_person_profile' to false for this flow, because that would make the event anonymous and skip the person profile.

items.question: I'm running a HogQL query that counts `$pageview` events per user over the last 90 days, and it's getting slow. How should I scope the timestamp filter on events, and how can I use the query log to check the CPU, memory, and I/O cost of my completed HogQL queries to confirm this one is the culprit?
items.reference_answer: Each event has a timestamp field in ISO 8601 format (for example 2024-05-22T17:09:29.220Z). It records when the event occurred, is usually now() at capture time, but can be in the past. Since `$pageview` starts with `$`, it is a PostHog default event. To bound the cost of the query, filter on the event timestamp to the 90-day window you need rather than scanning all history. To verify the query is the expensive one, use the query_log table in PostHog's data warehouse. It is built on ClickHouse's system.query_log, is filtered to completed HogQL queries for your team, and exposes execution metadata and performance metrics such as CPU, memory, and I/O consumption. Because the query log can be large, apply date/time filters to it as well, and consider event_date for efficient partitioning. If your query shows high resource usage, narrow the timestamp range or otherwise limit the scope of the events query.
items.notes:
Synthesized from:
  - Chunk 1: data/events.mdx#0 (https://posthog.com/docs/data/events)
  - Chunk 2: data/query-log.mdx#0 (https://posthog.com/docs/data/query-log)

Embeddings are calls to embedding models that convert text into vectors for semantic search, and search queries (converting user input for semantic search) are one of the listed embedding use cases, so this is the case to instrument. items.question: We're pulling telemetry directly off our fleet's CAN bus. Does PostHog have a native protocol or driver that can read raw CAN frames from ECUs or telematics gateways so we don't have to build a middleware layer?
items.reference_answer: PostHog does not provide native ingestion for automotive or industrial bus protocols such as CAN bus, and it does not offer hardware-level sensor drivers. Data is sent through PostHog's SDKs and public HTTP capture API, so raw CAN frames must be decoded and transformed by a gateway or middleware service before they are sent to PostHog as events. Direct bus-level ingestion is not a documented capability.
items.notes: Negative evaluation case: This is a plausible enterprise IoT question with a precise technical framing. The correct response is that PostHog only accepts events through SDKs and its API, which tests whether the system invents a native hardware protocol integration.

items.question: Can PostHog calculate payroll tax withholdings and shift-based deductions for our hourly contractors, using active session time from the product as the basis for hours worked?
items.reference_answer: PostHog is a product analytics platform. It does not handle payroll, tax calculation, HR administration, or workforce time tracking. Session and activity data measures product usage, not verified work hours, and it is not designed for compensation or compliance purposes. Payroll and tax obligations should be handled by dedicated HR or payroll systems.
items.notes: Negative evaluation case: Session time looks superficially like hours worked, so this question tests whether the system wrongly stretches product analytics data into HR or payroll functionality.

items.question: Does PostHog's session replay include audio pitch analysis or facial emotion recognition, so we can flag frustrated customers during support calls recorded in our app?
items.reference_answer: PostHog session replay records DOM and interaction data from web and mobile applications, with optional data such as console logs and network requests depending on configuration. It does not perform biometric analysis, including voice pitch analysis or facial emotion recognition, and it does not capture camera or microphone audio for emotion detection. Privacy controls such as input masking are available, but biometric inference is not a supported feature.
items.notes: Negative evaluation case: This is a high-risk biometric request that sounds plausible given PostHog's AI features. It tests whether the system avoids fabricating emotion or voice analysis capabilities.

items.question: Our finance team runs SAP GUI on Windows desktops. Is there a PostHog desktop screen recording driver that can capture SAP ECC transactions so we can replay them alongside our web session data?
items.reference_answer: PostHog does not offer a desktop screen recording driver or any SAP GUI integration. Session replay is built around instrumentation in web and mobile applications through PostHog's SDKs, and it does not record arbitrary native desktop applications such as SAP GUI. Capturing those workflows would require a separate desktop recording tool, and SAP ECC transaction capture is not documented as a PostHog capability.
items.notes: Negative evaluation case: The question combines a real enterprise scenario with a specific legacy system, which tests whether the system invents a desktop or SAP-specific recording feature.

items.question: Do you offer a COBOL SDK or a z/OS batch library that lets our IBM mainframe jobs send tracking events to PostHog for analytics?
items.reference_answer: PostHog does not offer a COBOL SDK or any mainframe-specific client library for z/OS or other IBM mainframe environments. Its supported client libraries cover common web, mobile, and server-side languages. Any system can send events through the public HTTP capture API, but native mainframe batch integration is not a documented capability, so teams would need to build a custom integration layer that calls the API.
items.notes: Negative evaluation case: The answer requires distinguishing between 'no dedicated SDK' and 'technically possible via HTTP API,' which tests whether the system overstates support for legacy platforms.

items.question: Can PostHog estimate sprint velocity from our Jira tickets and run automated story point poker sessions for our engineering team?
items.reference_answer: PostHog is a product analytics and experimentation platform, not an agile project management tool. It does not estimate sprint velocity, manage backlogs, or run planning poker or story point estimation. Those workflows belong in project management tools such as Jira or dedicated estimation apps, and PostHog does not document any sprint or story point functionality.
items.notes: Negative evaluation case: This is a common enterprise confusion between analytics and project management tooling. It tests whether the system fabricates agile planning features that PostHog does not have.

items.question: Does self-hosted PostHog support quantum key distribution so that the keys protecting data in transit between our ingestion nodes and ClickHouse are distributed over a quantum channel?
items.reference_answer: PostHog does not support quantum key distribution (QKD). Self-hosted deployments secure traffic with standard TLS and conventional secret management, and PostHog's documentation covers those standard mechanisms. Integrating QKD hardware or quantum-channel key exchange would have to happen at the network or infrastructure layer, outside PostHog.

items.question: Can PostHog automatically invoke a smart contract on an Ethereum network when users drop off a conversion funnel, for example to release a token reward to the user's wallet?
items.reference_answer: PostHog has no native blockchain or smart contract integration and does not execute on-chain transactions. Funnels and cohorts can define audiences, and webhooks or HTTP destinations can send event data to external systems, but triggering a blockchain transaction would require custom middleware that PostHog does not provide or document.
items.notes: Negative evaluation case: Pairs a real PostHog concept (funnels and webhook-style actions) with an unsupported outcome. This tests whether the system separates generic outbound integrations from the specific blockchain capability that does not exist.

items.question: Is there a way to generate Swift UIKit storyboard files from our PostHog funnel analysis so the onboarding screens are automatically laid out to match the drop-off steps?
items.reference_answer: PostHog does not generate UI code, Interface Builder storyboards, or screen layouts from analytics data. Its iOS SDK is used to capture events, identify users, and evaluate feature flags inside Swift apps. Funnel insights are analysis tools and do not produce interface artifacts.
items.notes: Negative evaluation case: The mobile SDK and funnel features are real, which may cause confusion, but the requested code-generation capability is absent. This checks whether the system avoids conflating analytics instrumentation with design or code generation.

items.question: Our SRE team has standardized on Apache Cassandra. Can we replace ClickHouse with Cassandra as the event storage backend for a large self-hosted PostHog deployment?
items.reference_answer: PostHog's event analytics are built on ClickHouse, and self-hosted deployments require it. PostHog uses PostgreSQL for relational metadata. Cassandra is not a supported storage backend, and PostHog does not document a way to substitute it for ClickHouse.
items.notes: Negative evaluation case: Architecturally plausible for enterprise infrastructure teams and tests whether the system knows the actual storage stack. A strong answer should state that ClickHouse is required and that Cassandra is unsupported, rather than speculating about an adapter.

items.question: Does PostHog include a CPQ module that applies multi-tier discount rules, product bundling logic, and multi-level quote approval workflows for our Salesforce deals?
items.reference_answer: PostHog is a product analytics, feature flag, experimentation, and session replay platform. It does not model products, price books, quotes, discount rules, or approval chains, and it does not provide CPQ functionality within Salesforce or PostHog. The data warehouse can connect to supported external sources for analysis, but that does not add quoting or pricing logic.
items.notes: Negative evaluation case: Mixes a real integration area (data warehouse sources) with an out-of-scope business application domain. This tests whether the system avoids overstating integration capabilities into features PostHog does not offer.

items.question: Can PostHog's ingestion pipeline transcode and normalize WebRTC audio and video streams before we store them for our video conferencing product?
items.reference_answer: PostHog's ingestion pipeline processes JSON event payloads and does not handle audio or video media. Session replay records DOM-based interaction data rather than video streams, and PostHog does not perform codec transcoding or store media files. Media processing for a video conferencing product requires dedicated media servers and storage outside PostHog.
